newsitem.title: FRANCE: Goering said he used criminals to loot Jewish art.
newsitem.headline: Goering said he used criminals to loot Jewish art.

text.p: Herman Goering boasted in a letter to another Nazi leader that he used French detectives and criminals to track down hidden art treasures belonging to French Jews.

"I obtained them from hiding places that were very difficult to find...by means of bribery and the employment of French detectives and criminal agents," Goering wrote to Alfred Rosenberg on November 21, 1940.
The letter was found in the U.S. National Archives in Washington and made available to Reuters in Paris on Wednesday by the European Jewish Congress.
Goering, who looted art treasures across Europe for the Nazi regime and for his private collection, offered no details about the people he employed.

But specialists said they believed he was referring to groups such as the notorious "Bony-Laffont" gang which hunted down Resistance fighters and Jews for the Nazis in exchange for immunity to continue its criminal activities during the German occupation of France.
Inspector Bony was a top pre-war Paris police detective who became so close to the criminals he was supposed to track that he became involved in their activities and was sacked.
Henri Laffont was a major gangland figure who ran nightclubs and brothels in the Pigalle area of Paris.

Their gang, at the service of the Germans' Gestapo secret police, was known for torturing its captives to make them reveal where their valuables were hidden. Both Bony and Laffont were executed after the war.

European Jewish Congress head Serge Cwajgenbaum said he released the Goering letter and other documents to shed further light on "the extremely courageous decision" by France this week to create a commission to investigate seizures by the Nazis and their Vichy French collaborators from 1940 to 1944.

Other documents shown to Reuters included an order from German army headquarters dated October 17, 1943, allowing searches of the quarters or homes of German officers "for the purpose of seizing art objects formerly in Jewish possession".

"The Nazis looted but they didn't want to be looted by their own people. Quite a number of German officers took advantage of their position to carry out illegal seizures in the homes of Jews who didn't know the difference and would not file complaints even if they knew," Cwajgenbaum said.
Another document concerned the creation of "Special Commmando" units designated to seize art works from Jews and remove anti-Nazi books and documents from public libraries.

The document goes into minute detail about the uniforms the units should wear, their allocation of fuel and the use of army telephone lines. It even gave the units the right to comandeer combat troops to back them up.
